media.title: How do we subtract one expression from another?
media.context: Expressions using Letter-Numbers. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Six pairs of expressions are subtracted by writing the second expression, then minus the bracket of the first. The minus sign before the bracket changes every sign inside it.

video_script.why: A learner uses the method of opening a bracket: the sign before the bracket acts on every term inside it, and then like terms are joined.

marks.p1: the title card From your book arrives
marks.p2: six pairs of expressions appear
marks.p3: an arrow shows the first expression being taken away from the second
marks.p4: a question mark glows beside the pairs

narration: <bookmark mark='p1'/>This question is from your book.
<bookmark mark='p2'/>It gives six pairs of expressions, and in each pair we subtract one from the other.
<bookmark mark='p3'/>The first expression in each pair is taken away from the second.
<bookmark mark='p4'/>What is the answer for each pair?
beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; six pairs of expressions with the words from between them

marks.think: Kiko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.
beats.on_screen: the six pairs stay on the board

marks.g1: the second expression is written, then minus and a bracket around the first
marks.g2: every sign inside the bracket flips

narration: <bookmark mark='g1'/>We write the second expression, then minus the bracket of the first.
<bookmark mark='g2'/>The minus sign changes every sign inside that bracket.
beats.on_screen: second expression − (first expression) ; the minus sign changes every sign inside the bracket

marks.gv1: the six pairs are written one under the other

narration: <bookmark mark='gv1'/>Given, six pairs of expressions in the letters eigh, b, x, y, g and h.
beats.on_screen: Given: (a) 9a − 6b + 14 from 6a + 9b − 18 ... (f) 8g + 4h − 10 from 7h − 8g + 20

narration: <bookmark mark='fd'/>We subtract in every pair.
We work the same way as the example in your book.
beats.on_screen: To find: the second expression minus the first, for each pair

marks.s1a: the second expression is written, then minus the bracket of the first
marks.s1b: every sign inside the bracket flips

narration: <bookmark mark='s1a'/>First, the first pair.
We write six eigh plus nine b minus eighteen.
Then we write minus the bracket nine eigh minus six b plus fourteen.
<bookmark mark='s1b'/>The minus sign changes every sign inside the bracket.
It becomes minus nine eigh plus six b minus fourteen.
<bookmark mark='s1c'/>Six eigh minus nine eigh is minus three eigh.
Nine b plus six b is fifteen b.
<bookmark mark='s1d'/>Minus eighteen minus fourteen is minus thirty two.
The answer is minus three eigh plus fifteen b minus thirty two.

marks.s2a: the bracket is written with a minus sign before it, and its signs flip

narration: <bookmark mark='s2a'/>Second, the second pair.
Flip every sign in the bracket being taken away.
<bookmark mark='s2b'/>Three x plus fifteen x is eighteen x, and seven y plus nine y is sixteen y.
<bookmark mark='s2c'/>Minus ten minus thirteen is minus twenty three.
The answer is eighteen x plus sixteen y minus twenty three.

marks.s3a: the bracket is taken away and its signs flip

narration: <bookmark mark='s3a'/>Third, the third pair.
Taking away seventeen g plus nine minus seven h flips all three signs.
<bookmark mark='s3b'/>Minus ten g minus seventeen g is minus twenty seven g.
Three h plus seven h is ten h.
<bookmark mark='s3c'/>Eleven minus nine is two.
The answer is ten h minus twenty seven g plus two.

marks.s4a: the bracket in the second expression is opened
marks.s4b: the first expression is taken away and its signs flip
marks.s4d: the b terms are joined and the answer is written

narration: <bookmark mark='s4a'/>Fourth, open the bracket in the second expression of the fourth pair first.
It becomes six eigh minus nine b minus eighteen.
<bookmark mark='s4b'/>Then we take away nine eigh minus six b plus fourteen, so its signs flip.
<bookmark mark='s4c'/>Six eigh minus nine eigh is minus three eigh.
<bookmark mark='s4d'/>Minus nine b plus six b is minus three b.
The answer is minus three eigh minus three b minus thirty two.

marks.s5a: the fifth pair is worked with signs flipped
marks.s5b: the sixth pair is worked with signs flipped

narration: <bookmark mark='s5a'/>Fifth, the last two pairs.
In the fifth, minus three x minus ten x is minus thirteen x.
<bookmark mark='s5c'/>Minus three y minus ten y is minus thirteen y.
<bookmark mark='s5d'/>Eight minus two is six, so the answer is minus thirteen x minus thirteen y plus six.
<bookmark mark='s5b'/>In the sixth, seven h minus four h is three h.
<bookmark mark='s5e'/>Minus eight g minus eight g is minus sixteen g.
<bookmark mark='s5f'/>Twenty plus ten is thirty, giving three h minus sixteen g plus thirty.

marks.s6a: 1 replaces eigh and b in the first pair
marks.s6b: the two expressions give minus 3 and 17
marks.s6c: the answer minus 20 matches the formula

narration: <bookmark mark='s6a'/>Sixth, check the first pair with eigh as one and b as one.
<bookmark mark='s6b'/>The second expression gives six plus nine minus eighteen, which is minus three.
The first gives nine minus six plus fourteen, which is seventeen.
<bookmark mark='s6c'/>Minus three minus seventeen is minus twenty.
Minus three plus fifteen minus thirty two is also minus twenty.

marks.ans2: the six answers are boxed one by one

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Every pair has now been subtracted.
<bookmark mark='ans2'/>The six answers are boxed on the board.

never_show: the differences before their steps
maths_rules: subtracting A from B means B - (A); the minus sign changes every sign in A
video_script.payoff_line: Every pair has now been subtracted

final_answer.spoken: minus three eigh plus fifteen b minus thirty two; eighteen x plus sixteen y minus twenty three; ten h minus twenty seven g plus two; minus three eigh minus three b minus thirty two; minus thirteen x minus thirteen y plus six; three h minus sixteen g plus thirty

video_script.substitution: The method of opening a bracket such as two times the bracket y minus one, with a minus sign before the bracket in place of the number two.

The second is fifteen x minus two x.
<bookmark mark='p4'/>What situation could each one describe?

marks.think: Kiko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

narration: <bookmark mark='s1a'/>First, the story for eight x plus three y.
<bookmark mark='s1b'/>A fruit seller sells mangoes at eight rupees each and bananas at three rupees each.

Together the bill is eight x plus three y rupees.

marks.s3b: x rupees is written on each pencil and 15x on the packet

The full packet is worth fifteen x rupees.

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Each expression now has its own story.
<bookmark mark='ans2'/>The first is fruit bought by a customer.
The second is a packet of pencils with two left unsold.

media.description: A pattern of squares starts with five squares and gains four squares at every step. The count is four n plus one, which gives seventeen, forty one and two hundred and one, and the vertices follow as sixteen n plus four.

content.text:
$1$. The Jowar roti brings in $30$ rupees for each of $x$ plates, so $30x$.
$2$. The pulao brings in $20$ rupees for each of $y$ plates, so $20y$.
$3$. The total earned is the sum $30x + 20y$, option $(a)$.
$4$. The wrong options fail because: $(b)$: charges $50$ for every plate of either kind; $(c)$: swaps the prices; $(d)$: adds only $y$ once; $(e)$: subtracts. Check with $x = 1$ and $y = 1$: $30 + 20 = 50$ for option $(a)$, but option $(b) = 100$ and option $(e) = 10$.
Answer: $(a)$: $30x + 20y$

content.text:
$1$. Every customer gets one flag, whatever they bought.
$2$. The customers are $p$ who bought only champak, $q$ who bought only marigold, and $r$ who bought both.
$3$. A customer who bought both is still one customer, so $r$ is counted once.
$4$. Flags $= p + q + r$, option $(a)$.
$5$. Check with $p = 3$, $q = 4$, $r = 2$: $9$ customers, and $p + q + r = 9$, while $p + q + 2r$ would be $11$.
Answer: $(a)$: $p + q + r$

content.publication_text: A snail is trying to climb along the wall of a deep well. During the day it climbs up $u\text{ cm}$ and during the night it slowly slips down $d\text{ cm}$. This happens for $10$ days and $10$ nights. $(a)$: Write an expression describing how far away the snail is from its starting position. $(b)$: What can we say about the snail's movement if $d > u$?

content.text:
$1$. $(a)$: In one day and night the snail moves $u - d\text{ cm}$.
$2$. For $10$ days and $10$ nights the distance is $10 \times (u - d) = 10(u - d)$ centimetres.
$3$. $(b)$: If $d > u$, then $u - d$ is negative, so every day and night ends lower than it began.
$4$. The snail slips down more than it climbs, so it never reaches the top.
Answer: $(a)$: $10(u - d)$ centimetres; $(b)$: it slips down more than it climbs, so it never reaches the top

content.publication_text: Radha is preparing for a cycling race and practices daily. The first week she cycles $5\text{ km}$ every day. Every week she increases the daily distance cycled by $z\text{ km}$. How many kilometres would Radha have cycled after $3$ weeks?

content.text:
$1$. Week $1$: $5\text{ km}$ a day for $7$ days is $5 \times 7 = 35\text{ km}$.
$2$. Week $2$: the daily distance is $5 + z$, so $(5 + z) \times 7 = 35 + 7z\text{ km}$.
$3$. Week $3$: the daily distance is $5 + 2z$, so $(5 + 2z) \times 7 = 35 + 14z\text{ km}$.
$4$. Total $= 35 + (35 + 7z) + (35 + 14z) = 105 + 21z\text{ km}$.
Answer: $105 + 21z\text{ km}$

$1$. One square needs $4$ matchsticks. Each new square joined to the row adds $3$ matchsticks.
$2$. For $10$ squares: $4 + 3 \times 9 = 4 + 27 = 31$ matchsticks.
$3$. For $w$ squares: $4 + 3 \times (w - 1) = 4 + 3w - 3 = 3w + 1$ matchsticks.
$4$. Check $w = 10$: $3 \times 10 + 1 = 31$.
Answer: $31$ matchsticks for $10$ squares, and $4 + 3(w - 1) = 3w + 1$ for $w$ squares

content.text:
$1$. The cycle has $4$ positions: red at $1$, yellow at $2$, green at $3$, yellow at $4$, then it repeats.
$2$. Divide each position by $4$. Remainder $2$ or $0$ means yellow, remainder $1$ means red, remainder $3$ means green.
$3$. $90 \div 4$ leaves remainder $2$, so yellow. $190 \div 4$ leaves remainder $2$, so yellow. $343 \div 4$ leaves remainder $3$, so green.
$4$. Red is at $4n - 3$, yellow is at $2n$ (every even position), green is at $4n - 1$.
Answer: Positions $90$ and $190$ are yellow, $343$ is green; red at $4n - 3$, yellow at $2n$, green at $4n - 1$

$1$. Step $1$ has $5$ squares and each step adds $4$, so Step $n$ has $5 + (n - 1) \times 4$ squares.

$4$. Each square has $4$ vertices, so vertices $= 4 \times (4n + 1) = 16n + 4$.
Answer: $17$, $41$ and $201$ squares; the formula is $4n + 1$; vertices $16n + 4$

$2$. Simplify: $5 + 4n - 4 = 4n + 1$.
$3$. Step $4$: $4 \times 4 + 1 = 17$. Step $10$: $4 \times 10 + 1 = 41$. Step $50$: $4 \times 50 + 1 = 201$.
$4$. Each square has $4$ vertices, so vertices $= 4 \times (4n + 1) = 16n + 4$.
Answer: $17$, $41$ and $201$ squares; the formula is $4n + 1$; vertices $16n + 4$

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M3.S32.T32.C156.IMG1}}
$1$. $(a)$: Row $r$ starts after $r - 1$ full rows of $4$ numbers. Column $1$: $4(r - 1) + 1$, column $2$: $4(r - 1) + 2$, column $3$: $4(r - 1) + 3$, column $4$: $4(r - 1) + 4$.
$2$. $(b)$: $124 \div 4$ leaves remainder $0$, so $124 = 4 \times 30 + 4$, giving $r - 1 = 30$ and $c = 4$: row $31$, column $4$. $147 = 4 \times 36 + 3$: row $37$, column $3$. $201 = 4 \times 50 + 1$: row $51$, column $1$.
$3$. $(c)$: The number in row $r$ and column $c$ is $4(r - 1) + c$.
$4$. $(d)$: Multiples of $3$ fall in the columns $3$, $2$, $1$, $4$, then repeat $3$, $2$, $1$, $4$.
$5$. Other patterns: every number in column $4$ is a multiple of $4$; even numbers appear only in columns $2$ and $4$; odd numbers appear only in columns $1$ and $3$.
Answer: $(a)$: $4(r - 1) + c$ for column $c$; $(b)$: $124$ at row $31$ column $4$, $147$ at row $37$ column $3$, $201$ at row $51$ column $1$; $(c)$: $4(r - 1) + c$; $(d)$: multiples of $3$ follow the columns $3$, $2$, $1$, $4$ repeating; column $4$ holds multiples of $4$; even numbers sit in columns $2$ and $4$; odd numbers in columns $1$ and $3$

(b) 124 ÷ 4 leaves remainder 0, so 124 = 4 × 30 + 4, giving r − 1 = 30 and c = 4: row 31, column 4. 147 = 4 × 36 + 3: row 37, column 3. 201 = 4 × 50 + 1: row 51, column 1.
(c) The number in row r and column c is 4(r − 1) + c.
(d) Multiples of 3 fall in the columns 3, 2, 1, 4, then repeat 3, 2, 1, 4.
Other patterns: every number in column 4 is a multiple of 4; even numbers appear only in columns 2 and 4; odd numbers appear only in columns 1 and 3.

content.text:
Summary
Algebraic expressions are used in formulas to model patterns and mathematical relationships between quantities, and to make predictions.
Algebraic expressions use not only numbers but also letter-numbers. The rules for manipulating arithmetic expressions also apply to algebraic expressions. These rules can be used to reduce algebraic expressions to their simplest forms.

content.text:
1. Our opening question is settled: a letter-number for the changing number of coconuts and another for the kilograms of jaggery give one short rule for any order.
2. Like terms add into one term; unlike terms stay apart; a minus sign before a bracket changes the sign of every term inside.
3. Patterns such as the saree border, the calendar and the matchsticks have formulas, and an expression can prove a pattern for every case at once.
4. Still open for you: invent a rule of your own, write it as an expression, and challenge a friend to find it.

objectives.objective_text: Students write a rule linking two ages with letter-numbers, replace the letter-number by a number to find the other age, and write the rule in reverse.
Students count the matchsticks for several numbers of Ls, describe the pattern in words, and write the expression 2 × n for any number of Ls.
Students turn a plain-words relationship into an algebraic expression, choose their own letter, and use the expression for a few values.
Students find the cost of one order, write the expression c × 35 + j × 60 for any order, and evaluate it for new quantities, reading it as a sum of two terms.
Students write the perimeter of a square as 4 × q, evaluate it for a given side, and name a general relation written with letter-numbers a formula.
Students turn a situation told in words into an expression by naming the changing quantities, writing each part, and joining the parts, then check it with a few numbers.
Students evaluate seven arithmetic expressions by writing their terms, converting each term to a number, using swapping and grouping, and opening brackets that have a minus sign outside.
Students evaluate arithmetic expressions with brackets and mixed signs by listing terms, swapping and grouping, and checking the value by solving the bracket first.
Students describe a sequence of multiples, find its third and 29th terms, and write the nth term as 4n by skipping the multiplication sign.
Students find the value of 7k when k is 4 and of 5m + 3 when m is 2, reading 7k as 7 × k and following the usual order of operations.
Students check nine claimed values, spot the slip in each wrong one, say what might have gone wrong, and give the correct value, including with negative values and brackets.
Students replace each letter-number in an expression by a given number, write the product when a number and a letter sit together, and evaluate carefully with negative numbers and brackets.
Students write the perimeter of a rectangle as a sum of its sides, swap and group the terms to get 2l + 2b, and check that both expressions take the same value.
Students write the money earned from each item as a multiple of its price, add the terms using the distributive property, and explain why 18c + 11d cannot be simplified further.
Students find the area of a big rectangle in two ways, reading 4v + 3v as 7v and 12n − 4n as 8n, and name sets of terms as like or unlike terms.
Students sort the terms of an expression into like groups, add each group into one term, and test that the simplified form takes the same values as the original for a few numbers.
Students write the amount paid minus the amount returned as two brackets, open the second bracket by changing every sign, and group like terms to a simplified expression.
Students read what 7p − 3q means, evaluate the three round scores for given p and q, add the expressions to get the total, and subtract two totals to see how much more one scored.
Students open a bracket with the distributive property, treat the last term as a negative term, and group like terms to simplify 4(x + y) − y.
Students open brackets that have a plus or a minus sign outside, or a number outside, and then group like terms to reach the simplest form.
Students replace the letter-number by several numbers in two expressions, compare the values, and decide from different values that 5u is not 5 + u and 10y − 3 is not 10(y − 3).
Students add the numbers in a picture in three different ways, row by row, by like terms, and by doubling the upper half, and see that all three simplify to 2r + 2s + 24.
Students check eleven claimed simplest forms, spot which are wrong and what slip may have caused each, correct them, and compare the number of terms with the number of letter-numbers.
Students add the numbers in a picture in more than one way, write and simplify the expression, and simplify a list of expressions with brackets and mixed signs.
Students study the inputs and outputs of a number machine, say its rule in words, write the rule as an expression, and check that it works for every set of inputs.
Students find the rule of two further number machines from several sets of inputs, write each as an expression in a and b, and write the expression for each set of inputs.
Students invent a rule on two letter-numbers, write number machines for it with several inputs, and challenge a classmate to find the rule.
Students find a machine's rule from its inputs and outputs, write it as an expression, and use it to find new outputs.
Students write the position of the nth appearance of designs C, B and A as 3n, 3n − 1 and 3n − 2, and explain why B and A sit one and two places before a multiple of 3.
Students divide a position number by 3, read the remainder, and decide which design appears at positions 99, 122 and 148.
Students find the design at a given position from the remainder on division by 3, and give the position of the nth appearance of each design.
Students find that the diagonal sums of a marked 2 by 2 square are equal, write the other three dates in terms of the top left date a, and prove that both sums are 2a + 8.
Students add the five dates in a cross shape on the calendar, see that the sum is 5 times the centre, and prove it for every cross by naming the centre a.
Students choose a shape on an endless calendar, name its centre a, write the other dates in terms of a, and show that the sum is always a multiple of a number in the shape.
Students count matchsticks in a growing triangle pattern, use the 2 added at each step to reach far steps, and write the formula 3 + 2 × (y − 1) and its simplified form 2y + 1.
Students count horizontal and diagonal matchsticks at each step separately, write an expression for each in terms of y, and check that the two add up to 2y + 1.
Students find the formula for a growing pattern from its first steps, simplify it, and use it for far steps and for other questions about simplifying, adding, subtracting and describing expressions.
Students restate how letter-numbers and expressions describe relationships, how like terms are added to reach simplest forms, and how expressions model and prove patterns.

Book item: Shabnam is 3 years older than Aftab. Write an expression for Aftab's age using s for Shabnam's age, and find it when Shabnam is 20 years old.
Book item: Each L in Parthiv's pattern uses 2 matchsticks. Find the sticks for 5, 7 and 45 Ls, then write an expression for n Ls.
Book item: Coconuts cost 35 rupees each and jaggery costs 60 rupees per kg. Find the total to pay for 10 coconuts and 5 kg of jaggery.
Book item: Write an expression for the total to pay for c coconuts and j kg of jaggery, then use it for 8 coconuts and 9 kg of jaggery.
Book item: Use the expression c × 35 + j × 60 for 7 coconuts and 4 kg of jaggery, and name its two terms.
Book item: Write an expression for the perimeter of a square with side q, and use it for a side of 7 cm.
Book item: Write formulas for the perimeter of: (a) a triangle with all sides equal. (b) a regular pentagon (a regular figure has all side lengths and all angles equal). (c) a regular hexagon.

Book item: Munirathna has a 20 m long pipe. He wants a longer watering pipe for his garden, so he joins another pipe of some length to this one. Give the expression for the combined length of the pipe. Use the letter-number k to denote the length in metres of the other pipe.

Book item: What is the total amount Krithika has, if she has the following numbers of notes of 100, 20 and 5 rupees? Complete the table, where each row gives the number of 100 rupee notes, the number of 20 rupee notes and the number of 5 rupee notes: row 1 is 3, 5 and 6 notes. Row 2 is 6, 4 and 3 notes (already worked: 6 × 100 + 4 × 20 + 3 × 5 = 695). Row 3 is 8 notes of 100, 4 notes of 20 and z notes of 5. Row 4 is x notes of 100, y notes of 20 and z notes of 5.

Book item: Venkatalakshmi owns a flour mill. It takes 10 seconds for the roller mill to start running. Once it is running, each kg of grain takes 8 seconds to grind into powder. Which of the expressions below describes the time taken to grind y kg of grain, assuming the machine is off initially? (a) 10 + 8 + y (b) (10 + 8) × y (c) 10 × 8 × y (d) 10 + 8 × y (e) 10 × y + 8
Book item: Write algebraic expressions using letters of your choice. (a) 5 more than a number. (b) 4 less than a number. (c) 2 less than 13 times a number. (d) 13 less than 2 times a number.
Book item: Describe situations corresponding to the following algebraic expressions: (a) 8 × x + 3 × y (b) 15 × j − 2 × k
Book item: In a calendar month, a 2 by 3 grid full of dates is chosen: 2 rows and 3 columns. Write expressions for the dates in the blank cells if the bottom middle cell has date w.
Book item: Evaluate 23 − 10 × 2, then 7 × 4 + 9 × 6, then 20 + 8 × (16 − 6).
Book item: Evaluate 83 + 28 − 13 + 32 by swapping and grouping, and then 34 − 14 + 20.
Book item: In the sequence 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, ... find the third term and the 29th term, then write the nth term.
Book item: Find the value of 7k when k = 4.
Book item: Find the value that 5m + 3 takes when m = 2.
Book item: Check these claims. 1: if a = −4, then 10 − a = 6. 2: if d = 6, then 3d = 36. 3: if s = 7, then 3s − 2 = 15.
Book item: Check these claims. 4: if r = 8, then 2r + 1 = 29. 5: if j = 5, then 2j = 10. 6: if m = −6, then 3(m + 1) = 19.
Book item: A rectangle has length l and breadth b. Write its perimeter as a sum of sides, simplify it, and check with l = 3 and b = 4.
Book item: Pencil sales on three days are 5, 3 and 10, each at price c. Simplify the total for pencils, and find it when c = 50 rupees.
Book item: Eraser sales on three days are 4, 6 and 1, each at price d. Write and simplify the total for erasers, then the total for pencils and erasers, and say whether it can be simplified further.
Book item: A big rectangle of height v is split into two rectangles of widths 4 and 3, with areas 4v and 3v. Write the area of the big rectangle in two ways.
Book item: A rectangle ABCD of height n and width 12 has a piece EBCF of width 4 cut off. Write the area of the piece AEFD that is left in two ways, and say which pairs are like terms.

Book item: A shop charges 40 rupees per chair and 75 rupees per table, and returns 6 rupees per chair and 10 rupees per table. Find the amount paid for x chairs and y tables, and say if (40x + 75y) + (−6x − 10y) is the same.

Book item: In the quiz, p = 4 is the score for a correct answer and q = 1 is the penalty for a wrong one. Say what 7p − 3q means, find Charu's three round scores 7p − 3q, 8p − 4q and 6p − 2q, and say what q would be with no penalty.
Book item: Find Charu's final score as an expression by adding her three round scores 7p − 3q, 8p − 4q, 6p − 2q, and check it when p = 4 and q = 1.
Book item: Krishita's final score is 23p − 7q. Give three round scores that could add up to it, and find how much more she scored than Charu, whose score is 21p − 9q.
Book item: Simplify 4(x + y) − y.
Book item: Replace u by 11, 8, 2 and 5 in 5u and in 5 + u, and say whether the two expressions are equal.
Book item: Replace y by 2, 10, 0 and 7 in 10y − 3 and in 10(y − 3), and say whether the two expressions are equal.
Book item: A picture has a top row of four 3s, then two rows each with one r and one s, and a bottom row of four 3s. Add all the numbers in three ways and simplify.
Book item: Check claims 1 to 4. 1: 3a + 2b = 5. 2: 3b − 2b − b = 0. 3: 6(p + 2) = 6p + 8. 4: (4x + 3y) − (3x + 4y) = x + y.

Book item: Add the numbers in each picture below. Write the corresponding expressions and simplify them. Try adding the numbers in each picture in a couple of different ways and see that you get the same thing. Picture (i) has two rows of three numbers: the top row is 5y, −6, x and the bottom row is x, 2, 5y. Picture (ii) has four copies of 2p, four copies of 3q, and the numbers 3, −2, −2 and 3. Picture (iii) has four copies of −5g and twelve copies of 5k.

Book item: Simplify each of the following expressions: (a) p + p + p + p (b) p + p + p + q (c) p + q + p − q (d) p − q + p − q (e) p + q − p + q (f) p + q − (p + q) (g) p − q − p − q (h) 2d − d − d − d (i) 2d − d − d − c (j) 2d − d − (d − c) (k) 2d − (d − d) − c (l) 2d − d − c − c
Book item: A Y-shaped number machine gives these results: inputs 5 and 2 give 8; 8 and 1 give 15; 9 and 11 give 7; 10 and 10 give 10. Find its formula and check it, including on the inputs 6 and 4.
Book item: A machine gives: inputs 5 and 2 give 5; 8 and 1 give 7; 9 and 11 give 18; 10 and 10 give 18. Find its formula, and write the expression for each set of inputs and for a and b.
Book item: A machine gives: inputs 4 and 1 give 5; 6 and 0 give 1; 3 and 2 give 7. Find its formula, then write the expression for inputs 10 and 3, and for a and b.
Book item: Make a formula of your own with letter-numbers a and b, write four number machines for it, and show the rule hidden for a classmate to find.
Book item: The border repeats A, B, C. Write the position of the nth appearance of C, B and A, and list the first three positions of each.
Book item: Find the design at positions 99, 122 and 148 by dividing each position by 3.
Book item: In the calendar square with 12, 13 on the top and 19, 20 below, add the two diagonals, then show that the diagonal sums are equal for every 2 by 2 square by calling the top left date a.
Book item: Check the expression 2a + 8 on another square whose top left date is 9, and say why a table of examples is not enough to be sure.
Book item: Add the cross of dates 8, 14, 15, 16, 22 and compare with the centre, then prove the pattern for any cross with centre a.
Book item: Find another shape on the calendar whose sum is a multiple of one of its numbers: a row of three dates with the middle date a.
Book item: Find the number of matchsticks in Step 5, Step 33, Step 84 and Step 108, using the 2 added at each step.
Book item: Write a formula for the matchsticks in Step y in two ways, and show they are equal by simplifying.
Book item: Count the horizontal and diagonal matchsticks in Steps 2, 3 and 4, then write an expression for each orientation in Step y and add them.

Book item: One plate of Jowar roti costs 30 rupees and one plate of Pulao costs 20 rupees. If x plates of Jowar roti and y plates of pulao were ordered in a day, which expression(s) describe the total amount in rupees earned that day? (a) 30x + 20y (b) (30 + 20) × (x + y) (c) 20x + 30y (d) (30 + 20) × x + y (e) 30x − 20y

Book item: Pushpita sells two types of flowers on Independence day: champak and marigold. p customers only bought champak, q customers only bought marigold, and r customers bought both. On the same day, she gave away a tiny national flag to every customer. How many flags did she give away that day? (a) p + q + r (b) p + q + 2r (c) 2 × (p + q + r) (d) p + q + r + 2 (e) p + q + r + 1 (f) 2 × (p + q)

Book item: A snail is trying to climb along the wall of a deep well. During the day it climbs up u cm and during the night it slowly slips down d cm. This happens for 10 days and 10 nights. (a) Write an expression describing how far away the snail is from its starting position. (b) What can we say about the snail's movement if d > u?

Book item: Radha is preparing for a cycling race and practices daily. The first week she cycles 5 km every day. Every week she increases the daily distance cycled by z km. How many kilometres would Radha have cycled after 3 weeks?

Book item: A figure shows ovals that hold expressions and boxes that hold operations, joined by paths. Along one path the expression w + 2 becomes 4w + 20. Fill in the missing blanks on the remaining paths. The other paths use the operations multiply by 3, subtract 8, subtract 4 and subtract 4, starting from w + 2 and w − 3, and the missing ovals are to be found.

Book item: A local train from Yahapur to Vahapur stops at three stations at equal distances along the way. The time taken in minutes to travel from one station to the next station is the same and is denoted by t. The train stops for 2 minutes at each of the three stations. (a) If t = 4, what is the time taken to travel from Yahapur to Vahapur? (b) What is the algebraic expression for the time taken to travel from Yahapur to Vahapur? [Hint: Draw a rough diagram to visualise the situation]

Book item: Simplify the following expressions: (a) 3a + 9b − 6 + 8a − 4b − 7a + 16 (b) 3(3a − 3b) − 8a − 4b − 16 (c) 2(2x − 3) + 8x + 12 (d) 8x − (2x − 3) + 12 (e) 8h − (5 + 7h) + 9 (f) 23 + 4(6m − 3n) − 8n − 3m − 18

Book item: Add the expressions given below: (a) 4d − 7c + 9 and 8c − 11 + 9d (b) −6f + 19 − 8s and −23 + 13f + 12s (c) 8d − 14c + 9 and 16c − (11 + 9d) (d) 6f − 20 + 8s and 23 − 13f − 12s (e) 13m − 12n and 12n − 13m (f) −26m + 24n and 26m − 24n

Book item: Subtract the expressions given below: (a) 9a − 6b + 14 from 6a + 9b − 18 (b) −15x + 13 − 9y from 7y − 10 + 3x (c) 17g + 9 − 7h from 11 − 10g + 3h (d) 9a − 6b + 14 from 6a − (9b + 18) (e) 10x + 2 + 10y from −3y + 8 − 3x (f) 8g + 4h − 10 from 7h − 8g + 20
Book item: Describe situations corresponding to the following algebraic expressions: (a) 8x + 3y (b) 15x − 2x

Book item: Imagine a straight rope. If it is cut once as shown in the picture, we get 2 pieces. If the rope is folded once and then cut as shown, we get 3 pieces. Observe the pattern and find the number of pieces if the rope is folded 10 times and cut. What is the expression for the number of pieces when the rope is folded r times and cut?
Book item: Look at the matchstick pattern of squares in a row. Observe and identify the pattern. How many matchsticks are required to make 10 such squares? How many are required to make w squares?

Book item: Have you noticed how the colours change in a traffic signal? The sequence of colour changes repeats red, yellow, green, yellow, then red again. Find the colour at positions 90, 190, and 343. Write expressions to describe the positions for each colour.

Book item: Observe the pattern of squares that grows with each step: Step 1 has 5 squares, and each step adds 4 squares. How many squares will be there in Step 4, Step 10, Step 50? Write a general formula. How would the formula change if we want to count the number of vertices of all the squares?

Book item: Numbers are written in a particular sequence in this endless 4-column grid: row 1 holds 1, 2, 3, 4; row 2 holds 5, 6, 7, 8; and so on. (a) Give expressions to generate all the numbers in a given column (1, 2, 3, 4). (b) In which row and column will the following numbers appear: (i) 124 (ii) 147 (iii) 201 (c) What number appears in row r and column c? (d) Observe the positions of multiples of 3. Do you see any pattern in it? List other patterns that you see.

chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's own order: a sweet shop with a different order every day opens the need for a short rule, letter-numbers give the rule, and simplifying then patterns put it to work. Every story is a video that ends on a question the student answers before the idea is named, and an interactive tool appears only where handling the expression is the idea itself.

points.text: The hook video leaves the laddu order question open. The word letter-number arrives only after the student has seen that the way to work out the bill stays fixed while the numbers change.
points.title: Try first, name later

points.text: Each idea gets its own topic: story or concept videos, one per concept, a closing practice concept (with a tool where handling the expression is the concept), then the book's Figure it Out questions in their own topic, one question and one video per concept.
points.title: Concept, then practice, topic by topic

points.text: Every expression is first said in plain words, then written with letter-numbers, then tested by replacing the letter-numbers by numbers.
points.title: Say it in words first

points.text: Like terms and brackets reduce an expression to its simplest form, and the same moves let an expression prove that a calendar or matchstick pattern holds for every case.
points.title: Simplify, then generalise
